passages.t: ‘God arises’: the father of the fatherless marches from Sinai
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “For the choirmaster. A Psalm of David. A song” (verse 1). It opens like a battle cry. “God arises. His enemies are scattered, and those who hate Him flee His presence” (verse 1).

Then a call to sing, and one of the tenderest lines in the Psalms. “A father of the fatherless, and a defender of the widows, is God in His holy habitation. God settles the lonely in families; He leads the prisoners out to prosperity” (verses 5 and 6).

The psalm looks back to the wilderness. When God marched before his people, “the earth shook and the heavens poured down rain before God, the One on Sinai” (verse 8). Kings fled, and women at home shared the plunder (verse 12).

The great mountains of Bashan look on in envy at the hill God chose (verses 15 and 16). His chariots are countless (verse 17). And he goes up in triumph. “You have ascended on high; You have led captives away. You have received gifts from men, even from the rebellious, that the LORD God may dwell there” (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
Verse 1 repeats what Moses said whenever the ark of the covenant set out in the wilderness: “Rise up, O LORD! May Your enemies be scattered” (Numbers 10:35). Verses 7 and 8 are close to the song of Deborah (Judges 5:4-5). Many readers think the psalm was sung as the ark was carried in procession into Jerusalem.

Verse 4 calls God the one “who rides on the clouds” (verse 4). Old poems from Ugarit, a city on the Syrian coast, gave the storm god Baal the title ‘rider of the clouds’. The psalm gives that title to Israel's God. He, not Baal, brings the rain (verse 9).

Bashan was the high country east of the Sea of Galilee, with mountains far taller than Zion. The picture is funny and pointed: the big mountains are jealous of a small hill, because God chose it.

A conqueror going up to his city led captives and received tribute. That is the picture in verse 18.

Fatherless children and widows had no one to defend them in law or in the market. The psalm says God himself takes that place.
passages.later:
Paul quotes verse 18 of Jesus going up to heaven: “When He ascended on high, He led captives away, and gave gifts to men” (Ephesians 4:8). The gifts he means are people given to the church to serve it.

Jesus promised his friends, “I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you” (John 14:18). James says true religion includes caring “for orphans and widows in their distress” (James 1:27).
passages.hard:
Notice that Paul's words differ from the psalm's. The psalm says God ‘received’ gifts. Ephesians says he ‘gave’ them. It is honest to say so. Readers account for it in a few ways. An old Aramaic translation used by Jews, the Targum, also reads ‘gave’, and applies the verse to Moses giving the law. So Paul may be following a way of reading the verse that already existed. Others point out that a conqueror received tribute and then gave it out to his people, so receiving and giving belong together. Peter said something like it of Jesus: he “received from the Father the promised Holy Spirit and has poured out what you now see and hear” (Acts 2:33).

More generally, Psalm 68 is one of the hardest texts in the Hebrew Bible. It has rare words and sudden jumps, and some lines (such as verse 13) are very uncertain. Bibles differ, and that is not a sign of carelessness.
passages.asks: If you grew up without a father, or feel alone, verse 5 is for you. God calls himself ‘a father of the fatherless’. Verse 6 adds that he ‘settles the lonely in families’. Often he does that through his people. A church can be that family. And if you have a home, who could you make room for?

passages.t: ‘Who daily bears our burden’, and kingdoms singing to God
passages.happening:
This half begins with praise for a God who is close. “Blessed be the Lord, who daily bears our burden, the God of our salvation” (verse 19). “Our God is a God of deliverance; the Lord GOD is our rescuer from death” (verse 20).

Then fierce words about God's enemies (verses 21 to 23).

Then the procession. “They have seen Your procession, O God” (verse 24). Singers lead, musicians follow, and young women play tambourines (verse 25). Tribes from the south and the north march together (verse 27).

The psalm ends wide. Kings will bring gifts to the temple (verse 29). “Envoys will arrive from Egypt; Cush will stretch out her hands to God” (verse 31). “Sing to God, O kingdoms of the earth” (verse 32). Its last word is “Blessed be God!” (verse 35).
passages.hearers:
‘Daily bears our burden’ can also be read ‘daily carries us’. Either way, God is not only a warrior far off. He carries his people every day.

Tambourines and women singing go back to the exodus, when “Miriam the prophetess, Aaron’s sister, took a tambourine in her hand” (Exodus 15:20). The tribes named in verse 27 come from the far south (Benjamin and Judah) and the far north (Zebulun and Naphtali). The whole people is in the parade.

Cush was the land south of Egypt, along the upper Nile. To the first hearers it stood for the far edge of the known world. Even there, people would reach out their hands to God.
passages.later:
Luke tells of an official from Ethiopia, the land south of Egypt, who “had gone to Jerusalem to worship” (Acts 8:27) and was baptised on his way home. Readers have long seen verse 31 coming true in him.

Paul writes that Christ, on the cross, “disarmed the powers and authorities” and triumphed over them (Colossians 2:15).
passages.hard: Verses 21 to 23 speak of crushed heads and feet dipped in the blood of enemies. They are among the war pictures of the Psalms. The book page's part on the cursing psalms explains how Christians read lines like these, and that no reading of them makes it right to harm anyone.
passages.asks:
Verse 19 is a good verse to learn. You do not carry your load alone. God carries it, or carries you, ‘daily’: today, and again tomorrow.

The psalm ends with the whole earth singing. The God of Sinai and Zion is not a local god. He wants Egypt and Cush and every kingdom. Where do you see that happening now?
